title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Greece in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Greece in 10 Minutes
description:
From the first Olympics to the Roman conquest, this is the whole story of ancient Greece in about ten minutes: the alphabet, Homer and the Trojan Horse legend, naked Olympians, Athenian democracy and ostracism, Spartan training, Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis, the Parthenon, the Peloponnesian War, the trial of Socrates, Alexander the Great and the fall of Corinth. Every fact is checked.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #ancientgreece #greekhistory #sparta #animatedhistory

beats.say: August, 480 BC. A narrow pass in northern Greece, squeezed between the mountains and the sea.
Coming toward it is the biggest army anyone in Greece has ever seen: the army of King Xerxes of Persia.
Blocking the pass are about seven thousand Greeks, led by Leonidas, one of Sparta's two kings.

show.label: Greeks holding the pass at first

beats.say: There are so many Persian archers, their arrows will block out the sun!
Good news. Then we'll fight in the shade.
That joke comes from Herodotus, a Greek historian who wrote it down a few decades later. They held the pass for two days.
Then a local man showed the Persians a path around the mountain. Leonidas sent most Greeks home and stayed with his three hundred Spartans, plus hundreds of other Greeks.
Almost all of them were killed. So how did a bunch of squabbling Greek cities end up shaping the whole Western world? Let's start at the beginning.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Ancient Greece in 10 Minutes
show.sub: From the first Olympics to the Romans

beats.say: First, the map. Greece is mostly mountains, islands and sea, so its people never formed one country.
Instead there were hundreds of city-states, little countries of one city plus its farms. Each had its own laws, army and attitude.
Greece had just come out of a dark age. Around 1100 BC its old palace kingdoms collapsed, and for centuries nobody wrote anything down.
Then, around 800 BC, Greeks borrowed letters from the Phoenicians, sea traders from what's now Lebanon, and added vowels. Hello, alphabet.
Soon the poet called Homer, if he was one real person, gave Greece its greatest stories: the Iliad and the Odyssey.
They're about the Trojan War. The famous wooden horse full of soldiers? That's a legend, and it isn't even in the Iliad.
And in 776 BC, at Olympia, the first recorded Olympic Games had exactly one event: a sprint of about two hundred meters.
I'm a cook, and I just won the Olympics. Dinner's on me!
Every four years, Greek cities even declared a truce, so athletes and fans could travel to the Games safely.
Later, Olympic athletes competed completely naked. That's where we get the word gymnasium: gymnos means naked.

show.label: Greek word of the day
show.sub: = naked. A gymnasium was a place to exercise naked.

beats.say: The two big city-states were Athens and Sparta, and they were total opposites.
In 508 BC, an Athenian leader named Cleisthenes set up a new system: the citizens themselves would vote on the big decisions.
They called it democracy, rule by the people. But only free adult men counted. Women and enslaved people got no vote at all.
Athenians who skipped politics were called idiotes, meaning private people. That's where our word idiot comes from.
They could even vote a politician out of town. Each man scratched a name on a piece of broken pottery.
With at least six thousand votes, the most-named man had to leave Athens for ten years. That's called ostracism.

show.label: Votes needed to ostracize someone
show.sub: the loser left Athens for 10 years

beats.say: The most famous story, from the Greek writer Plutarch, is about a politician nicknamed Aristides the Just.
Excuse me, I can't write. Could you scratch the name Aristides on my shard?
Sure. What did he ever do to you?
Nothing. I'm just sick of hearing everyone call him the Just.
So Aristides wrote his own name. He was voted out, though Athens called him back a few years later to fight Persia.
Sparta, meanwhile, was one big army camp. Boys left home at seven for brutal training, and were fed so little they were expected to steal food.
If they got caught, they were beaten. Not for stealing. For getting caught.
Next door was the Persian Empire, the biggest empire the world had ever seen, stretching from Egypt to India.
In 490 BC, Persian ships landed at Marathon, a beach near Athens. The Athenian army marched out to meet them, and won.
Herodotus counted one hundred ninety-two Athenians dead, against sixty-four hundred Persians.
The story of a runner dashing to Athens to announce the win, then dropping dead, is a later legend. It still gave us the marathon race.
Ten years later, Xerxes came back with a much bigger army. That's when Leonidas made his stand at Thermopylae.
Herodotus claimed it had over two million men. Modern historians think it was far smaller, but still huge.
After it, the Persians marched in and burned Athens. But the Athenians had already escaped by sea.
Their general, Themistocles, had built a big navy. He lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait at Salamis, and smashed it.
A year later, the Greeks won again on land, and Persia never invaded mainland Greece again.
Victory made Athens rich and bossy. Its leader Pericles, always painted wearing his helmet, spent the money on art.
In 447 BC, Athens started the Parthenon, a giant marble temple to the goddess Athena. It still stands on the hill above the city.
Some of that money came from other Greek cities. They'd paid Athens to protect them from Persia, and Athens wouldn't let them quit.
This is when Athens invented theater, with comedies and tragedies, and when philosophers started asking big questions.
But Sparta didn't like Athens getting so powerful. In 431 BC, they went to war. It's called the Peloponnesian War, and it lasted twenty-seven years.
A plague hit crowded Athens and killed perhaps a quarter of the people, including Pericles himself.
In 404 BC, Athens surrendered. Sparta had won.

show.title: Socrates Asks One Question Too Many

beats.say: Now meet Socrates, a philosopher who walked around Athens asking people questions until they realized they didn't know anything.
Lots of people found that very annoying. In 399 BC, he was put on trial for disrespecting the gods and corrupting young people.
A jury of about five hundred citizens voted. A majority said guilty. Then each side proposed a punishment.

show.label: Socrates' jury
show.sub: and most of them voted guilty

beats.say: So, Socrates, what punishment do you think you deserve?
Honestly? Free dinners for life, like an Olympic champion.
That's really what he asked for, according to his student Plato. The jury was not amused, and sentenced him to death by hemlock, a poison.
He drank it calmly, surrounded by friends. Plato wrote down one of his most famous lines from the trial.

show.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.

beats.say: While the big cities wore each other out, a kingdom in the north got strong: Macedon, led by King Philip the Second.
In 338 BC he beat Athens and Thebes in battle, and most of Greece fell in line. Sparta didn't, so Philip sent a threat.
If I invade your land, I will drive you out!
If.
That's the story told by Plutarch, a Greek writer centuries later. And Philip never did take Sparta.
In 336 BC Philip was murdered, and his twenty-year-old son became king. He'd been taught by the philosopher Aristotle.
We know him as Alexander the Great. He crossed into Asia, beat the Persian armies again and again, and took Egypt, where he founded Alexandria.
In about eleven years he built an empire from Greece to India, and never lost a battle. His favorite horse, Bucephalus, even got a city named after him.
In India, his exhausted soldiers finally refused to go any further, so he turned back.
Then, in 323 BC, he caught a fever in Babylon and died at just thirty-two. His generals split the empire and fought over it for decades.
Still, Greek language and ideas now stretched across the whole region. Greek cities kept inventing amazing stuff.
Archimedes, a genius from Syracuse, a Greek city in Sicily, supposedly jumped out of his bath shouting Eureka, meaning I found it. That one's probably a legend.
Sadly, when Roman troops captured Syracuse in 212 BC, Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier.
And around this time, someone built the Antikythera mechanism: a box of bronze gears you cranked to predict eclipses. It's been called the world's oldest computer.
But a new superpower was rising in Italy: Rome.
Roman legions beat the Macedonians, and in 146 BC, after a Greek revolt, a Roman general named Mummius destroyed the city of Corinth.
From then on, Greece was ruled by Rome.
But the Romans fell in love with Greek gods, statues, plays and books. A Roman poet named Horace joked that captive Greece had captured its conqueror.
So that's ancient Greece: squabbling cities that gave us democracy, the Olympics, philosophy, theater and the word idiot. Not bad for a bunch of rocky islands.
Next up: the entire history of France. See you there.
